1:
Why these two tribes had so much cattle is asked before anything else, and answered by guesswork. Gill says it is not easy to say by what means they came to have more in proportion than the rest, and supposes they were more addicted to the pastoral life, took more delight in breeding and were more diligent in the care of their beasts. Henry reports the common supposition, that they brought more out of Egypt than the others did, and rejects it on the arithmetic: that was forty years before, and stocks of cattle increase and decrease in less time than that; he prefers better husbandry, that they had tended their flocks better and taken more care of the breed, and had not been so profuse as their neighbours in eating the lambs out of the flock and the calves out of the stall. On the land itself the geographers agree. Keil and Delitzsch note that Jazer is put first probably because that district was especially rich in pasture, place Gilead north and south of the Jabbok across two modern provinces, and observe that ancient Gilead still shows numerous traces of great fertility; Ellicott says the same of both districts and adds that even in its present desolation the traces remain. Wesley reduces it to a line, a city and country of the Amorites and a mountainous country famous for pasturage.

How the request came to be made at all is Henry's subject, and he draws a principle out of it. The affair was concerted not by any particular order or appointment of God but at the special instance of two tribes, to which Moses consented only after a long debate; and even at a time when so much was being done by the extraordinary appearances of divine Providence, many things were still left to the direction of human prudence, since God in governing both the world and the church makes use of the reason of men and serves his own purposes by it. He notes that Reuben and Gad encamped under the same standard and so had the better opportunity of comparing notes, and that although Reuben is named first in the opening verse Gad is named first afterwards — either because the Gadites made the first motion and were the most forward, or because they were the better spokesmen and had more of the art of management, Reuben's tribe still lying under Jacob's sentence that he should not excel. Gill reports the same reversal and cites Aben Ezra for the view that the Gadites were the authors of the counsel, having first moved it to the Reubenites who lay encamped beside them.
3:
Whether the petition was blameworthy divides into degrees rather than sides. Calvin condemns it most heavily and most carefully at once. He allows that the request was apparently reasonable, since God had driven out the inhabitants and the fertility invited them, and he calls their modesty praiseworthy, since they neither detached themselves from the people nor seditiously seized the places but sought them by permission; yet he holds that private interest had so laid hold of their minds that the main point did not occur to them, that their association for the war had been established by God and bound them by an indissoluble tie, and that the land of Canaan was assigned to the whole race of Abraham to be inhabited as a peculiar world. In asking for ground outside those limits they disunite themselves from the body of the Church as if they desired to be emancipated from God; and he takes the verb about seeing the land as a warning, that we beware lest our eyes by unlawful looks lead us into snares and blind our minds. Henry files the same motives under two heads, the lust of the eye and the pride of life, since the land was not only pleasant to look at but good for food. Ellicott judges more coolly that the language indicated a selfish consideration of their own interests and was calculated to discourage and dishearten their brethren.

What exactly they were asking for is the one point of real dispute. Keil and Delitzsch allow that the words about not crossing the Jordan may express nothing more than a wish that their inheritance should not lie on the western side, with no intention of withdrawing their help from the conquest, and they point to the men's own later declaration as evidence. Ellicott concedes that reading and then sets against it a stronger one: the words may equally be taken, as they appear to have been understood by Moses and as they were in all probability designed to be understood, as a request that the conquest of the western side be left to the other tribes altogether, the speakers perhaps judging from the ease and rapidity of the eastern conquest that their brethren could manage without them. He closes the question with a fact from long afterwards, that these two tribes and the half tribe of Manasseh were among the first taken into captivity by the king of Assyria. Keil and Delitzsch add the detail that makes the land so easy to ask for, that the clause about the country the Lord smote describes it as a land without a ruler, which could therefore be taken possession of without difficulty; and Gill, listing the towns, notes that one of them is named nowhere else in Scripture but in this chapter.
6:
What Moses is chiefly angry at is answered differently by each witness. Gill says he was displeased because the motion had at first sight an appearance of covetousness and cowardice. Henry names three faults together, a disregard to the land of Canaan, a distrust of the Lord's promise, and an unwillingness to encounter the difficulties and dangers of driving out its inhabitants, and turns the rebuke into a rule, that it ill becomes any of God's Israel to sit down unconcerned about the difficult and perilous concerns of their brethren, whether public or personal. Keil and Delitzsch order the charges as the speech orders them, want of brotherly feeling first and the discouragement of the others second, with the wrath of God as the consequence. Calvin ranks them explicitly and puts them the other way about: their ingratitude and perverseness towards God is chastised more severely than their injustice towards their brethren, since the effect of their request would be that the hearts of the children of Israel should be broken so that they refused the call of God.

Calvin also answers a question the others do not raise, whether the sharpness of the reproof was itself excessive. He argues that its very severity shows the greatness of the wrong, since neither did inconsiderate warmth carry Moses away into such violent anger nor did he err by pronouncing on a matter he did not understand; he knew what the two tribes were asking, and inveighed so vehemently because they desired to lacerate the body of the Church by this wicked severance. The injustice he puts plainly: they sought to indulge in idleness while their brethren marched through a hostile land, possessing no rightful superiority that would let them throw all the labours and perils and burdens of the war upon others, since God had imposed the same condition on all and united them so that they should keep company with each other. Wesley compresses the same contrast into a line, that they would sit in ease and peace while their brethren were engaged in a bloody war.

The verb for discouraging is examined by the philologists. Ellicott says the word rendered discourage means rather to alienate or to avert, and points to the cognate noun used in the same connection later in the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch render the idiom literally as holding the heart away, and explain the effect as taking from the other tribes both the courage and the inclination to cross over. Gill counts the practical loss as well as the moral one, that the army would forfeit the assistance of two tribes, two thirds of one of their standards, and that the request might be read as carrying a distrust of ever being able to conquer Canaan at all, which could not but discourage the rest.

The appeal to the fathers is made to do more work than it first appears. Gill notes that the fathers meant are not those of these two tribes only but of all the tribes alike, who would not go up when they were bidden but sent spies first. Calvin holds that the comparison doubles rather than excuses the guilt, since the imitation of ungodly parents is no defence, and cites the reproach that a later preacher made to his own hearers about resisting the Holy Ghost as their fathers did, and the Psalm that recalls the same provocation in the wilderness. He then makes a distinction the passage repays: Moses does not compare the Reubenites and Gadites to the whole people but to the ten spies from whom the sedition arose, because so far as in them lay they turned the people aside from the right way. He also stops on the phrase about not fulfilling after the Lord, and draws from it that there is nothing praiseworthy in the most vigorous course unless men persevere even to the goal.
10:
The oath and its forty years are recited rather than expounded, and the witnesses add only what the recital assumes. Gill takes the anger to have been kindled against the spies who brought the ill report and against all the people who were disheartened and murmured upon it. Ellicott notes that Moses is here declaring the fulfilment of the very prediction he had himself announced, in obedience to the divine commandment, at the time the evil report was brought up. Keil and Delitzsch supply the threat in the plainest terms, that if these men draw back behind God and resist his will to bring Israel to Canaan he will leave the nation still longer in the desert, so that they prepare destruction for the whole people; Gill glosses the turning away as a turning from following him in the way of his commandments, from his word and worship and ordinances, and from the pillar of cloud and fire that went before them.

One name in the list of the exempted starts a small genealogical dispute. The question is whether the epithet belongs to Caleb or to his father, and if to the father, how the descent runs. Gill argues for the father and gives his reasons: it does not suit to derive the name from the Kenaz who fathered Othniel, since Othniel is called Caleb's brother and they are unlikely to have been own brothers, Caleb having given him his daughter; and besides, it is always Jephunneh and never Kenaz who is named as Caleb's father. He concludes that both were called by the name from some remoter ancestor, and reports a rabbinic reading in which Caleb was rather Kenaz's son-in-law. Clarke states the first half of the same conclusion flatly, that it was Jephunneh who was the Kenezite and not Caleb, and supposes Kenaz was probably Jephunneh's father. Wesley takes the same descent one generation further back, that the name comes from Kenaz his grandfather.

The word for what the sons are to their fathers is where Calvin spends his effort, and he names the renderings he rejects. He takes it to mean an addition, and specifically a climax, holding that those translate poorly who render it education, or offspring, or foster-children; the Hebrew noun comes from a root meaning to increase and multiply, and is literally an increase or multiplication, being applied for that reason to usury. The passage, he argues, requires the sense of a heap: a new body of persons is springing up afresh who carry impiety to its very height, so that fuel is added to a fire already smouldering and a new flame is excited. The thought behind the word he takes to be the filling up of the fathers' measure, as it was said of a later generation. Gill reads the same clause more simply, that these men succeeded their fathers in their families, of which they were now the heads, and in their substance, their flocks and herds — and, Moses suggests, in their manners and evil dispositions too. Henry draws the moral the whole passage is pointed at, that if men considered as they ought what would be the end of sin, they would be afraid of the beginning of it.
16:
Whether the two tribes had meant this all along is a question the witnesses handle very differently. Henry raises it and refuses to settle it, drawing a separate lesson from each branch: if they did intend it from the first, it is an instance of how often what is honestly meant is unhappily misinterpreted, though Moses was excusable since he had reason to suspect the worst and rebuked them out of an abundance of care to prevent sin; and if they did not, it is an instance of the good effect of plain dealing, since by showing them their sin and its danger he brought them to their duty without murmuring or disputing. Calvin settles it the second way and makes the severity itself the cause: from their reply we gather how usefully the sharpness of Moses had worked upon their minds, since had he dealt with them more mildly his kindness would perhaps have been received with contempt, and it was more profitable that their stubborn hearts should be smitten with shame and fear. He observes too that they do not abandon the request but devise a middle course, and adds the one advantage they still keep, that by depositing their wives and children in a peaceful spot they would have the opportunity of improving their domestic finances. Gill notices only the manner of the approach, that the heads of the tribes came a little nearer with something more to say, and used some degree of freedom and boldness.

What they proposed to build is agreed to be rebuilding rather than founding. Ellicott says the word rendered build often means to build up or repair and probably means that here, and that the folds were commonly constructed of loose stones piled one upon another. Keil and Delitzsch say the same of both, that by the building of towns we are to understand their rebuilding and fortification, and describe the pens as stone walls piled up; they add a traveller's observation that the nomads of one district still ring each camp with an enclosure about the height of a man, so that the flocks may not scatter and so that the noise of the smaller stones laid on top will betray a wolf trying to enter in the night. Clarke reaches the same conclusion from impossibility, that these men could not have built and fortified cities in the time available, and cites Calmet for the view that they meant no more than repairing the cities of the Amorites they had lately taken.
17:
Whether every fighting man was really to go is the sharpest practical question in the chapter, and Clarke answers it with arithmetic. He asks first who was to defend the fortified cities if only women and children were left in them, and says it cannot be supposed possible, so that many of the men of war must have stayed behind; then he counts, taking the three tribal numbers from the last census and halving the third, to reach a total of a hundred and ten thousand five hundred and eighty men, against the forty thousand that the book of Joshua records as actually crossing over armed. The remainder, seventy thousand five hundred and eighty, he takes to have been left for the defence of the families and flocks, which he thinks more than sufficient against peoples already panic-struck. Wesley reads the promise as elastic from the outset, that they undertook to go either all or as many as should be thought necessary, leaving only enough to provide for the sustenance and defence of those behind. Clarke also names who the danger was from, the Ammonites, Moabites, Idumeans and the remains of the Midianites and Amorites, and Ellicott notes that the word for little ones seems to cover the whole defenceless portion of the nation, while Keil and Delitzsch set the undertaking out in its parts, the equipping in haste, the dwelling of the families in fenced cities, and the refusal to return home until every man in Israel had his inheritance.

The disclaimer in the nineteenth verse is read for its tone and for a critical question. Gill insists it was not said in contempt of the good land nor as a settled refusal, but as giving up all pretensions to any share there if their own request were granted. Ellicott agrees the language must not be interpreted as spoken in a defiant spirit, and then treats the verse as evidence of a different kind: it is one of the critical passages bearing on a word rendered here both as on yonder side and as on this side, and since the same word is applied to the country on both banks, nothing can be inferred with any degree of certainty from it about whether the writer stood east or west of the river.
20:
The phrase about going armed before the Lord draws the entry's closest reading. Ellicott infers that the army of Israel was regarded as the army of the Lord, and that the ark was carried into war on certain occasions; he supports it from the order of march, in which Reuben and Gad encamped on the south of the Tabernacle and immediately preceded the ark, and from the later scene in which the priests bearing it stood still in the river until all had passed over. He then observes who says what: if this is the true force of the phrase, it was natural that the Reubenites should first say only before the children of Israel, and not adopt the expression before the Lord until Moses had used it. Wesley reads the same words of the ark as the token of God's presence and allows either the order of the march or the manner of the passage as the allusion. Gill notes that Moses tries them thoroughly and is very express, requiring not merely a march but a crossing, and not some of them but all.

Calvin then raises an objection about Moses that no other witness raises, and raises it against himself. Moses might seem to err on the side of excessive good nature in extending the boundaries God had prescribed, since the promised inheritance was in Canaan and he was not allowed to alter a divine decree; and there is a second inconsistency no less serious, that in a point of so much perplexity he does not, as usual, consult God, but gives an immediate answer which indirectly overthrows the previous ordinance. Calvin then answers it from the outcome rather than the moment. God, who knows how to bring light out of darkness, not only pardoned the error but took occasion to extend his liberality, so that Bashan and its neighbourhood were added to the former boundaries, while showing how much better it would have been for the tribes to be kept together; and after a long period the two tribes learnt from experience that they had been too hasty in wishing for the land they obtained. That Moses was guilty of no rashness Calvin infers from two later facts: that he commands the arrangement to be maintained after his death, and that when the inheritances are assigned in the book of Joshua this country is excepted as already granted — from which his decision is evidently approved.

The warning that closes the terms is where two witnesses do their best work on a single sentence. Calvin treats it as a solemn protestation with a punishment annexed, as if Moses were summoning them before the tribunal of God, and draws the doctrine that unless we abide by our promises God will always avenge fraud and treachery. On the wording he is exact: the saying that sin will find them out is more emphatic than a plain statement that they shall not escape God's hand, because it means that vengeance is so connected with sin that it cannot be severed from it, as sin was said in an older text to lie at the door to lay hold at length of the guilty; and he adds that God's forbearance encourages us to audacity while we suppose we have escaped because for a time he makes as though he saw us not. Wesley turns the clause into a duty: the sin that finds a man out is the punishment of it, and it concerns us to find our sins out first, so as to repent of them and forsake them, lest they find us out to our confusion and destruction. Gill adds what the intervening verse assumes, that a people fleeing might well be said to be subdued before the Lord, the work being done in his presence, by his power, and for his own.
28:
The conditions Moses attaches are read as a legal instrument. Henry sets out the structure: Moses settles the matter with Eleazar and with Joshua who was to succeed him, knowing he would not live to see it perfected, and gives the tribes an estate upon condition, leaving it to Joshua to declare the estate absolute if the condition were met. He is careful about what the penalty would have been — not that they should have no inheritance at all, but that they should not have this one they coveted, being compelled instead to come over with the rest and take their lot among their brethren and fare as they fared. Calvin gives the same terms and the reason for them, that the conditions were annexed lest the two tribes should afterwards be falsely accused of having crossed the Jordan only to look for a new home, and lest, if they did deceive their brethren, their cowardice should profit them; the alternative allotment inside Canaan is not offered as a reward for inertness but as a compulsion, since they would be carried onwards authoritatively and made subject to their brethren in all circumstances. He adds an observation about the tone of the whole passage, that in laying down rules for a division of the land as though it were about to happen, Moses encourages everyone to confidence, as if the victory were already in their hands. Gill notes that the sentence reads as though Moses determined the case himself, and supposes it was rather by the vote and with the consent of the whole court; Calvin says the same, that though Eleazar and the elders are not mentioned it is certain they were not passed over, since the case had been brought before them from the beginning.

The answer of the two tribes is examined for a grammatical detail. Gill notes that the verb is in the singular and takes it to show their unanimity, that they answered all of them as one man, and that there may have been a single spokesman who was the mouth of them all. Wesley takes the clause about what the Lord has said two ways, either of the present moment through Moses, or of the older command that they should go into Canaan and possess it. Calvin, on the grant itself, insists that Moses acted relying on God's command and laid down an inviolable law, and that although the text does not say God interposed his authority, his subsequent approbation fully assures us of it; he also finds an implied contrast here between the old covenant made with Abraham and this new and special privilege.
32: Before the grant itself, Gill notices how the undertaking is worded, repeated again and again for the confirmation of it and to assure that it should be strictly performed according to its true intent, and wonders in what form the grant was made, whether by word of mouth in the presence of the court or rather by some instrument drawn up and signed by Moses and the elders, or witnessed by them; Keil and Delitzsch define what was conveyed with the precision of a deed, the land according to its towns and in its districts, that is, the whole of it with its towns and the districts surrounding them. The appearance of half Manasseh at the very end, after taking no part in the negotiation, is the one thing every witness finds odd. Keil and Delitzsch call it strange that the half tribe should be included here for the first time at the close, when it is not mentioned in the negotiations at all. Ellicott resolves it by pointing forward, to the verses that show a portion of that tribe had been chiefly if not exclusively engaged in conquering parts of Gilead and Bashan and had thereby justly acquired a claim to what they had subjugated. Henry offers three possibilities and settles on none — that they asked, or that it was by divine direction, or that they had signalized themselves in the conquest of the country — while noting that the land proved more than the two tribes needed, and adding a soldier's reason of his own, that men celebrated for courage were well placed in a frontier country. Calvin turns the oddity into a chronological question: the descendants of Machir and Jair and Nobah had already seized certain cities, and the reason this portion is excepted is that they were not to be defrauded of lands separately acquired. He rejects the reading that would put those conquests after the grant as unsuitable, since it is not probable men would afterwards make an incursion to appropriate what did not belong to them, and observes that it is common with the Hebrews to transpose the order of occurrences when something omitted is added to explain what follows — though he ends by conceding that if anyone prefers to think them attracted by an advantage that presented itself, he will not pertinaciously contend the point.
34:
That the cities were repaired and not founded is agreed by everyone, and each argues it differently. Gill says the wars with Sihon and Og had demolished walls and houses that now needed rebuilding, and presses the point from the calendar: Heshbon was a royal city and Elealeh stood within a mile of it, so these were places long in being, and besides, the tribes had only a few months before they crossed the Jordan — though he allows that they left men enough behind who could be set to work on the building when the rest departed. Wesley says they had neither need nor leisure to do more, the old cities not having been burnt and ruined as several in Canaan were. Ellicott argues from probability, that new cities would not have been built at this time and that the circumstances of the Israelites did not admit of the delay such an undertaking would involve. Keil and Delitzsch simply gloss the verb as restored and fortified. Henry gives the same reading and adds the alternative cause, that the Amorites may have suffered the places to go to decay.

The list of towns is where the geographers do their work. Keil and Delitzsch identify almost every name with a modern ruin or village and give distances for each: one an hour north of the central Arnon, another among extensive ruins on a hill between two named places, another surviving in ruins on the edge of a lofty rocky wall. They are willing to correct a colleague by name, rejecting an identification of Aroer with the Aroer before Rabbah in favour of the Aroer of Reuben in the middle of the Arnon valley; and they admit ignorance where it is due, one town being mentioned only here with its situation unknown. Of Heshbon they report ruins about a mile in circumference with deep bricked wells and a large reservoir, still bearing the ancient name. Gill supplies the local traditions instead, that one city is called in the Jerusalem Talmud by another form of its name and was renamed Livias or Julias by Herod, and that Kirjathaim is described in a Targum as the city of two streets paved with marble. Ellicott adds the one modern fact in the chapter, that it was at Dibon that the Moabite stone was discovered in 1868, and notes that in the later distribution some of the southernmost Gadite towns fell to Reuben while Heshbon fell to Gad and was assigned to the Levites.

Why the names were changed divides into three answers. Gill and Wesley agree on the religious reason: Nebo was the name of an idol and the other name means Baal's habitation, where there was very probably a temple, and the Reubenites would not retain such idolatrous titles — Wesley citing the rule that the names of other gods were not to be mentioned. Clarke gives a purely political reason, that those who conquered cities called them after their own names, and instances Kenath, which took the name of the man who took it. Henry offers both and does not choose, either to show their authority, so that the change of names should signify the change of owners, or because the old names carried a respect to the deities worshipped there. Gill adds the detail that undoes the whole operation, that the text does not say what the new names were, and that when the places later fell into the hands of the Moabites the ancient names were restored to them.
39:
Whether the conquests of Machir's children came before or after the grant is a question of tense, and it is settled the same way by three witnesses. Keil and Delitzsch say the imperfects are to be understood as pluperfects, the clauses being linked in the simple manner of Semitic historical writing, where the explanatory clauses precede the leading thought instead of being subordinated to it, so that the sense is that the sons of Machir had gone and taken Gilead, and Moses then gave it. Ellicott renders it so directly, that the children of Machir had gone to Gilead and taken it. Calvin reaches the same conclusion by argument rather than grammar, rejecting the reading that puts the victories after the permission as unsuitable and improbable, while conceding that he will not contend the point pertinaciously. Gill marks the distinction the verse depends on, that the Gilead territory the two tribes had asked for was already conquered, being the country the Lord had smitten before Israel, while the part given to half Manasseh was still in the hand of the Amorites until these men took it.

Two of the three men named at the close raise questions of descent. On Machir, Gill reports from Aben Ezra the opinion that he was still alive and received the grant himself, and rejects it on the rule that all who came out of Egypt aged twenty and upward died in the wilderness but two; Wesley says the same more shortly, that Machir was doubtless long since dead and the family is meant. On Jair the genealogy is stranger and all three of the closest readers agree about it: Keil and Delitzsch trace him to a father of the tribe of Judah who had married a daughter of Machir, so that the line went over into the maternal tribe against the ordinary rule, and they guess at the reason, that Machir had portioned his daughter with a rich dowry as though she were an heiress; Ellicott gives the same descent and calls him one of those Israelites reckoned as belonging to their mother's tribe; Gill puts it in a clause, that he was of Manasseh by his mother's side and otherwise of the family of Judah. On Nobah nobody can do better than a guess. Gill says who he was is not certain and thinks him very probably a descendant of Manasseh, relaying a tradition that he was born in Egypt and buried beyond Jordan; Keil and Delitzsch say his family is never referred to and suppose him a Machirite like Jair, and reject a proposed identification of his city with a village a traveller had described, preferring the site that later geographers assign to Decapolis, whose ruins still run three miles round.

The chapter ends on a verdict that three witnesses reach independently and that a fourth had already reached at the opening. Clarke, citing Ainsworth, sets the two facts side by side: these two tribes and a half were the first to have their inheritance assigned to them in the promised land, and they were also the first of all Israel to be carried captive out of it, because of their sins, being delivered into the hands of two named kings and carried to four named places. Wesley makes the same observation his closing remark, that as these tribes were placed before the others so they were displaced before them, carried captive some years earlier, and that providence frequently observes such a proportion in balancing prosperity and adversity. Ellicott had noted the same thing far back at the fifth verse, as a fact deserving notice. Clarke adds one point of translation that has nothing to do with it, that the name Jair gave his towns means the villages or habitations of Jair and ought to have been translated so rather than carried over untranslated.
